doc.title: Tim Ries interviewed by Monk Rowe, Utica, New York, March 19, 2022

title: Learning tunes to sit in: Rusty's in Toledo and Eddie Abrams
summary: Ries explains how he learned tunes sitting in at Rusty's club in Toledo with Eddie Abrams, Claude Black and other Detroit musicians.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: First paid gigs: pay, bands and young beginnings

blocks.x: I wanted to follow up way back, and you talking about sitting in in some of the places in Detroit when you were fairly young. How did you prepare to be ready for those moments? Because getting asked to sit in and then you get onstage and, “Well how about ‘Nardis’.” “No I don’t know that one.” Was there a way to get ready for that or did they let you suggest a tune?

Well luckily there was a really cool jazz club in Toledo, Ohio called Rusty’s. Her name was Rusty Monroe, and she had this club for many, many, many years. And she cooked the food. And I think I remember once like as she got older and she was telling me about how long it took for her to actually start making money as an owner of a jazz club. Because it was a very popular place, a lot of musicians who came through town — Joe Henderson played there, you know, and all the Detroit musicians would come down because it was really close, it was like less than an hour drive from Detroit to Toledo. So at that club, that’s where I first started going with my father who would drive me there. And there was a guy named Eddie Abrams, an old musician, and he would let all the young people come and sit in, like all of us who were 13, 14, 15, 16, like Ron Oswanski was playing when I started playing there when I was getting older, Ron was, he just turned 48 and so there’s 12, 13 years’ difference. So when he was a kid he would then come sit in with me. So I figured that’s how you learn. So Eddie would let me sit in for playing a blues and I would take a song that I would know and he’d go “What do you want to play, what do you know?” “How about this” “Okay let’s do that.” So he’d let me sit in. So as a kid, and then this guy named Claude Black, another pianist from the area let me sit in. So like Cass Harris, this trumpet player from Detroit, he would be playing. So they would let me sit in — Gene Parker, Jimmy Cook, then more, like I say Marcus Belgrave — so then you learn more and more tunes. And they were kind enough to let © Fillius Jazz Archive -20-

me, as a kid — what did I know, nothing. You know so they were very inviting, very like hey what do you know? So it was like okay, so the next time I go I’m going to learn two more songs, then three. Then you start learning more songs. And then eventually then I started playing with his band you know. In fact last night I did something and I ended this song a certain way and Ron says, “It sounds like an Eddie Abrams ending.” You know? So it was kind of a cool thing, because he had a particular thing and then there was another organist, a pianist that I used to play with in Detroit, just like a certain way of playing and vibe from the Detroit sound. It had its own thing.
